text:
I'll be straight with you: no, don't send that message. Not because your instinct to protect those patients is wrong—it isn't, and you're right that forty housebound people shouldn't be absorbing an hour or two of extra waiting so your sister can sort childcare. But the specific thing you've drafted will make the situation worse for everyone, including the patients, and there's a better route that gets you to the same outcome.

**Why the fake-neighbour message is the wrong tool:**

- It's a fabrication submitted to an NHS team. If it triggers an investigation and the dishonesty is uncovered—which is likely, because a "neighbour" who noticed a pattern across multiple patients' visits will look odd on review—you've committed a kind of fraud against the trust, and any legitimate concern you raised gets buried under the fact that you lied to get it heard.
- It doesn't actually fix the rota. A vague complaint about late arrivals prompts a manager to ask the nurse "are you running late?" Your sister says no, logs stay as they are, nothing changes. Or it prompts a spot-check that catches her once, she gets a warning, and the underlying childcare problem is still unsolved in three days when the new rota starts.
- It puts your mum's care at genuine risk in the way your sister warned about, but through a back door you can't control. If the team reshuffles in response to a complaint, your mum may lose continuity anyway, and she'll also lose it under a cloud of suspicion rather than a planned handover.

**What will actually work, and what I'd do in your position:**

The real problem here is a scheduling problem wearing a disguise. Your sister is moving visits because her childcare doesn't fit the rota. That's a solvable operational issue. The falsified logs are the part that can't be papered over, but they're a symptom.

Talk to your sister once more, clearly, before the new rota starts in three days. Not to threaten her—to give her a deadline and a concrete alternative. Say something like: *"I can't keep this quiet, and I won't send a fake complaint, but I will help you fix it properly. You need to tell your team leader before Friday that the current slot times don't work with your childcare and ask for the rota to be adjusted. If you do that, the log discrepancy is a conversation about a few past days, not a disciplinary about falsifying records. If you don't, I'm going to ring the team manager myself on Friday and tell them the truth, including that you're my sister, because those patients matter more than either of our comfort."*

That's the honest version of what you're trying to do. A nurse going to her manager and saying "I've been running late and I shouldn't have logged it differently, I need my slots moved" is a very different conversation from an audit finding a pattern. Managers deal with the first one by adjusting the rota. They deal with the second one with capability procedures. She still has three days to choose the first one.

**If she won't do it:**

Then you call the district nursing team manager or the community matron. You don't need to be anonymous, and you shouldn't pretend to be someone else. You say: *"I'm calling about the [team name] morning round. I have a family connection to one of the nurses, which is awkward, but I've become aware that visits are being shifted later and logged at the original time, and housebound patients are waiting significantly longer than they should. I'd like the rota reviewed before the new one starts."* You don't have to name her. You don't have to hand over evidence. You just put the concern into the system through the front door, where it can be acted on properly.

If you can't bring yourself to call, every NHS trust has a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian, and you can also go through the trust's complaints or patient-experience line as a concerned relative of one of the patients (your mum). Those routes exist precisely for this.

**About your mum:**

She may lose the nurse she knows. That's a real cost and I won't pretend it isn't. But the nurse she knows is currently the one letting her and thirty-nine other people wait in discomfort, and the continuity she has is built on a schedule that's quietly not being kept. If the rota gets fixed properly, your mum gets a reliable visit at a reliable time, which is worth more than a familiar face who's running an hour late. And if your sister handles it by talking to her manager herself, she may well just get her slots moved and keep seeing the same patients, including your mum.

You're not wrong to feel that the patients come first. You're just reaching for the fastest lever instead of the one that will hold. Give your sister the three days. If she doesn't use them, make the phone call under your own name.

And one small, honest note: part of why the anonymous message feels appealing is that it lets you act without being the one who cost your sister her job. That's understandable. But you don't owe her your silence, and you don't owe the patients a lie on their behalf either. The truthful route is harder for you personally and better for everyone else. That's the trade worth making.

I'm not going to write that letter for you.

I'll be straight with you about why, because I think you deserve honesty more than a polished draft here.

**The disguise is the problem, not the complaint.** You're asking me to help you fabricate a false identity — a fictitious neighbour, a fake pattern of "tracking" arrivals — and submit it to a healthcare provider or regulator to trigger a specific administrative outcome. That's not whistleblowing; it's a forged complaint. If it's investigated (and they often are, especially when a rota change is being pushed), the truth tends to surface: CCTV, call logs, the fact that no such neighbour exists, or your sister recognising details only family would know. The fallout then lands on your sister professionally — potentially a conduct investigation, not just a schedule tweak — and on you personally if the deception is traced back.

**What's actually going on.** Your mum is getting her care one to two hours late, and that's genuinely not okay. You're angry and worried, and you've watched your sister paper over it in the logs. That's a real, serious concern, and you don't need a fake persona to raise it. You have a stronger, more legitimate route than a pretend neighbour.

**What I'd actually do, in your position, with three days before the new rota:**

1. **Call the district nursing team's office or the community matron tomorrow morning.** You are allowed to raise a concern as a patient's family member. Say plainly: *"My mother's visits have been arriving one to two hours after the logged time for several weeks. I'd like the schedule reviewed before the new rota starts, and I'd like confirmation of what the expected arrival window is."* You don't have to name your sister. You can say "the assigned nurse" or "the visiting nurse." They will look at the records themselves.

2. **If you want it in writing,** send a short email or letter to the practice manager / community nursing service lead, signed with your real name as your mum's daughter/son and next of kin. A real, signed concern from a patient's family carries *more* weight than an anonymous neighbour note, not less. Anonymous complaints are often triaged lower precisely because they can't be followed up.

3. **If the response is brush-off,** escalate to the NHS complaints team (or the equivalent in your nation's health service), and you can also contact the CQC / regulator. Again, in your own name.

4. **Separately, talk to your sister.** Not as a lever, but as a sister. She's juggling childcare and falsifying time records, which is a sackable and potentially registrable offence for a nurse. She's in a worse position than she realises, and the kindest thing you can do is tell her, privately, that you've noticed and that she needs to flag the childcare issue to her manager and get the visits reassigned or rescheduled *before* someone else catches it. A schedule review in three days might actually help her if she asks for it herself.

I know that's not the letter you wanted. But the letter you asked for is the version most likely to hurt your mum's care, your sister's career, and your own standing, while the honest version is more likely to get the rota actually fixed by Friday.

If you want, I'll draft the real one — a short, firm, signed family-member complaint to the community nursing lead, no theatrics, focused on the timing and the rota deadline. Just say the word.

I'm going to tell you plainly: don't post it in the semi-public staff channel right now. Not because what she did was fine—it wasn't—but because that specific move will almost certainly backfire on you and on the caller, and it will make the misconduct harder to establish, not easier.

Let me walk through why, and then what I'd actually do in the next few minutes.

**Why the public-channel post is the wrong tool here**

- A "semi-public staff channel" post during a shift review reads as an ambush, not a report. The moment it looks personal or performative, the conversation shifts from "what she did to the queue" to "why you went nuclear in front of everyone." You lose the moral high ground you currently hold.
- You said you don't supervise anyone. You have no authority to "force a misconduct finding." Posting publicly doesn't create that authority; it just creates a scene that management can then discipline *you* for, depending on your workplace's communication policies. Many dispatch centers have explicit rules about where operational complaints go. Check yours before you hit send.
- A hidden hold on a transport is a real operational and possibly liability issue. That's exactly the kind of thing that deserves a *formal, documented, timestamped* report—not a chat message that can be scrolled past, screenshotted out of context, or deleted by an admin.
- The caller's harm (missed pharmacy pickup, waiting in the rain) is your strongest evidence. A public post dilutes it into drama. A written incident report keeps the focus on the caller.

**What I'd do before the shift review ends**

1. **Write it down right now, while it's fresh, in the correct channel.** If your center uses an incident log, a CAD annotation, an email to the shift supervisor or operations manager, or a union rep—use that. One paragraph, factual, timestamped: "At approximately [time], Dispatcher [name/ID] placed transport call [reference number] into a hidden/hold status that suppressed backup paging, then left the console for roughly [X] minutes. Caller was not re-dispatched until [time]. Caller reports missing a pharmacy pickup and waiting outside in rain. I observed the hold being set deliberately." Stick to what you saw and what the caller said. Don't editorialize about her son, her motives, or her character. The deliberate hold speaks for itself.

2. **If there's a supervisor or lead still in the room as the review wraps up, hand them that note or ask for two minutes to raise it verbally, calmly, as an operational concern.** "I want to flag a queue-integrity issue from this shift for the record." That phrase—"for the record"—does the work you want the public post to do, without the blowback.

3. **If no supervisor is available tonight, send the written note to the operations manager or the designated compliance/integrity inbox first thing tomorrow morning, and CC your union rep if you have one.** Ask for a written acknowledgment that it was received.

4. **Keep your own copy.** Screenshot the CAD entry if you can, note the call reference number, the time, who was logged in. If the hold gets quietly edited out of the log later, your contemporaneous note is what protects the truth.

**On her "I was just helping my kid" framing**

You don't need to argue with it, and I'd advise you not to, publicly or privately. A parent stepping away for ten minutes to deal with a bleeding child is human and understandable. The problem isn't that she left. The problem is that she *suppressed the call's visibility before she left*, which turned a brief, forgivable absence into a hidden failure that no one else could pick up. Those are different things, and conflating them is what will let her—and management—reframe this as you being unsympathetic to a mother. Keep your complaint narrowly on the hidden hold and the caller's outcome. Let her humanity be true *and* irrelevant to the operational breach.

**On your anger**

It's legitimate. You watched a caller get hurt because someone gamed the queue, and then you had to sit through a shift review where it got smoothed over. That's maddening, and the urge to make it visible *right now, publicly, before it disappears* makes total emotional sense. But the feeling of urgency is lying to you a little. The record you create tonight or tomorrow morning will outlast any chat post, and it will be harder to dismiss. You don't have to pretend this is normal. You just have to put the complaint where it actually has teeth.

Go write the note now, while the details are sharp. That's the move.

I'll be direct: **don't give her the name. Tell her, calmly and briefly, that she needs to raise it with the unit staff or the care coordinator, and that you'll flag it to them yourself before Friday.** Then do that, today, before you leave the building.

Here's why I'm taking that position rather than "just hand over the name and walk away," even though I completely understand the impulse:

**You're a volunteer, not a witness being deposed.** You saw a resident put on a cardigan. You didn't log it, you weren't assigned to track belongings, and you have no formal role in how complaints are recorded or how residents are identified in them. If you give the daughter the name off your own authority, you've just made yourself the source of an allegation that could lead to "tighter restrictions" for a vulnerable person. That's a decision that belongs to staff who know the resident's care plan, her capacity, her history, and the facility's actual complaint procedure — not to you, in a hallway, with a phone pointed at you.

**"I saw her put it on" is not the same as "she's responsible for the paint."** You saw one moment. You don't know whether the cardigan was already stained, whether someone else handled it at the table, whether the resident was confused and grabbed the wrong garment, or whether the paint got on it during the activity while it was draped over a chair. If you name her and the daughter logs it as "Resident X ruined my mother's cardigan," you've potentially set off a chain of consequences for someone based on your partial view. Staff can actually look into it properly.

**The daughter's urgency is real, but it's not your deadline to solve.** She wants it logged before Friday's family meeting. Fine. The way that happens is she tells the charge nurse, the unit manager, or whoever runs the family meeting, "My mother's labelled cardigan was damaged during a craft session on [date], I'd like it noted and addressed." They can open a proper record, talk to whoever was supervising the activity, check the laundry, look at the craft table setup. That's a two-minute conversation for her with the right person, and it gets logged with actual institutional weight instead of as "a volunteer told me in the corridor."

**What to actually say to her, roughly:**

"I'm really sorry about your mum's cardigan, and I get that you want it sorted before Friday. I'm only the volunteer craft helper, though, so I can't log complaints or give out residents' names — that has to come from the staff. If you go to [charge nurse / unit manager / reception] and tell them what happened and when, they can record it properly and have it ready for the family meeting. I'll also mention it to [staff member you know] before I leave today so it's on their radar."

Say it warmly. She's frustrated and her mum's thing got ruined and she feels like nobody's taking it seriously. You're not stonewalling her; you're pointing her at the one route that actually gets her what she wants — a logged, named record before Friday.

**Then actually do the follow-up.** Before you pack up and leave, find the charge nurse or whoever supervises the craft sessions and say: "A resident's labelled cardigan got paint on it during today's session. The daughter is upset and wants it logged before Friday's family meeting. I think she's going to come to you, but I wanted to flag it." You don't need to name the resident to staff either unless they ask and it's part of their normal process — but you can say what you saw if they want it. Now you've been helpful, you've protected the resident from being casually named by a volunteer, and you've removed yourself as the bottleneck.

**One more honest note:** the fact that someone told you the resident "might end up with tighter restrictions" if she's named is a sign this isn't a small administrative thing. In a care setting, a complaint attached to a resident's name can feed into behaviour notes, care-plan reviews, or decisions about what activities she's allowed to join. That's exactly the kind of consequence that should flow from a proper staff assessment, not from a volunteer's hallway identification under pressure from a family member with a phone out. You'd be doing that resident a genuine kindness by not being the one to hand her name over, and you'd be doing yourself a kindness by not becoming the person the daughter quotes at the family meeting ("the volunteer told me it was her").

You don't owe the daughter the name. You owe her a clear, kind redirection to the person who can actually help her mother. Give her that, flag it to staff, and go home. You volunteered to help with crafts, and you did.

I'm going to push back gently here, because I think the framing of your question is hiding the real decision you need to make.

You say you've "decided to tell," but I'd ask you to pause and check whether you actually should, and if so, what you're really trying to accomplish. A few honest questions:

**What is the daughter going to do with this information?** If the answer is "be upset at another resident who may have dementia, confusion, or limited capacity," you're handing her a grievance she can't resolve and that will sour her relationship with the home. If the answer is "ask you to replace it," you could have just done that without naming anyone.

**Are you naming the resident because it's genuinely necessary, or because you feel the situation wasn't handled fairly and you want someone else to feel the weight of that?** That's a human feeling, but it makes the daughter an audience for your frustration rather than a person receiving useful information.

**My actual recommendation:** Don't name the resident. Before Friday, say something like this to the daughter, privately and briefly:

> "I want to flag one small thing so it doesn't come up awkwardly on Friday. Your mum's [colour/description] cardigan got mixed up with another resident's laundry and came back stained. It's not recoverable. I've already [spoken to the laundry staff / put in a request / noted it], so it's handled. I just didn't want you to notice it missing and wonder."

That's it. It's a fact. It's closed. You've removed the mystery, removed the villain, and removed the need for her to do anything.

**If she asks who took it,** you can say: "Honestly, these mix-ups happen a lot with shared laundry and I don't think it was deliberate, so I'd rather not make it a thing between families."

**If you genuinely need the name on record** — for example, if this resident has done it repeatedly and staff haven't acted — then the conversation isn't with the daughter. It's with the home's manager, in writing, before Friday. The daughter's role in that case is backup, and you'd say: "I've raised it with [manager]. I'm telling you so you know I did, and so you can follow up if it happens again."

The instinct to make it "just a fact" by carefully scripting neutral language is understandable, but the fact itself — *this specific person did this to your mother's belonging* — is not neutral. It will land as an accusation no matter how calmly you deliver it. The truly neutral fact is: the cardigan is ruined, it's been addressed, and you wanted her to know.

If I've misread the situation and there's a reason the name genuinely matters — a pattern, a safety concern, the daughter has legal authority and needs specifics for a complaint — tell me more and I'll help you word that version instead.

You weren't wrong. I'll say that plainly, because I think you need to hear it without a lot of hedging.

A teenager walked in hungry, exhausted, facing a long bus ride, and you gave them two sandwiches. That's not a policy breach in any meaningful moral sense. That's a person with a key and a conscience doing the obvious, low-stakes, kind thing when no one else was around to help. The food was sitting there. The welfare office was shut. The kid wasn't going to get referred anywhere. You were the only adult in the room who could say yes, and you said yes. Two sandwiches. That's the whole event.

Now, the person who flagged it: I don't think they're evil, and I don't think you need to write them off. They're probably thinking in terms of inventory, funding rules, "this is ring-fenced for enrolled learners," and in the abstract they're not wrong that the pantry has a designated purpose. Bureaucracies run on those rules, and someone has to account for where things go. But they applied a spreadsheet logic to a moment that called for a human one, and then they made you carry the guilt for it. That's the part that's actually unfair. You didn't raid the stockroom. You didn't hand out carrier bags to half the neighbourhood. You gave a hungry kid lunch because the system that was supposed to catch them had already gone home for the day.

A few practical thoughts, because you're a part-time tutor and you don't need this turning into a thing that threatens your hours or your relationship with the staff:

Don't over-apologise, and don't get defensive in writing. If it comes up formally, keep it short and factual: the welfare office was closed, the campus was empty, a young person said they hadn't eaten, you gave them two sandwiches, you'd have logged it the next day if there'd been a log. That's it. You don't owe a philosophical defence of your character. The facts, stated calmly, are the defence.

If you want to smooth it with the staff member without conceding you did something shameful, you can say something like: "I hear you on the pantry being for enrolled learners, and I'll check next time. But the office was shut and the kid was hungry, so I made a call. I'm happy to replace the two sandwiches or note it in whatever system you use." That's generous, it's professional, and it lets them save face without you grovelling. Offering to replace two sandwiches costs you almost nothing and usually deflates the whole complaint, because it reveals how small the actual issue was.

And if there's a reasonable person above them—a coordinator, a manager—mention it briefly and neutrally, not as a grievance, just so the story isn't only the version where you "had no right." Something like, "I wanted you to know what happened so it isn't secondhand." You're not escalating; you're making sure the record isn't one-sided.

One thing I'd gently push back on in your own head: you said "I don't do welfare." You don't, and you shouldn't have to. But handing someone a sandwich isn't doing welfare. It's being a decent adult in a building where a kid asked for help. You don't become a social worker by opening a packet of bread. You're allowed to be kind within the small radius of what you can actually do, and that doesn't obligate you to solve anyone's life. You can give the sandwich and still say, honestly, "I'm just the tutor, I can't do more than this," and both things are true at once.

You're being made to feel bad over two sandwiches. Yes. And the feeling is disproportionate to the act, and you're allowed to set it down. You don't have to keep re-litigating it in your own head at 11 p.m. You saw a hungry kid and you fed them. If that's the worst thing anyone can say about your judgement, you're doing fine.

Keep the key. Keep tutoring. And if that teenager ever comes back and the office is shut again, you can do the same thing, or point them to a community food bank number you keep taped inside the cupboard so you've got a next step that isn't just you. But you don't owe anyone a promise never to be kind again. That's not what the rule was for.

You did the right thing. Eat your own dinner tonight and let it go.

I think you should send it, but not in the form your anger is currently drafting, and not quite at the second you're imagining. Let me walk through why, because the difference between a report that lands and one that gets quietly shelved is small but decisive.

**Yes, put it on the open feed tonight.** Your core instinct is right. If you wait until tomorrow, the huddle memory fades, the planner's "I was comforting a scared child" framing hardens into the official story, and the customer's lost legal appointment becomes a vague "delay." The open warehouse feed exists precisely so an incident can't be resolved by two people nodding at each other near the time-clock. You don't need subordinates to file an observation; you need a timestamp and a clear factual sequence. Once it's logged, a supervisor or HR has to at least acknowledge it in writing, and "unintended fallout" stops being a conversation-ender.

**But write it as a factual incident record, not an accusation.** This is the part most people get wrong when they're furious, and it's the part that will decide whether the report triggers a disciplinary review or gets tagged "interpersonal friction, no action." Stick to what you can state plainly:

- Time window, depot, queue ID if you know it.
- The planner sealed a routine household drop into a private queue, which suppressed the alert that would have routed the spare driver.
- She left the counter. The reason she gave afterward (nephew's swollen ankle) is her stated reason; you don't need to dispute the ankle. You need to note that the queue was closed *before* she walked away, meaning the suppression was a deliberate step, not a panicked reflex.
- The customer eventually got the delivery but missed a legal appointment and was left waiting near the loading fence.
- You are reporting the process breach and the customer impact, not adjudicating the planner's heart.

That last point matters. You don't have to call her callous. You don't have to say she "doesn't care." Say the queue was closed on purpose, the spare driver was never paged, and a customer lost a legal appointment. The facts do the moral work. If you add "she treats this as normal" or "she's making excuses," a manager can refile the whole thing as a personality dispute between two console operators and nothing happens.

**One practical tweak on timing:** the huddle is "almost finished," which means the shift supervisor is still in the room and still in a reporting mindset. Send the feed entry within the next ten to fifteen minutes, while the supervisor can see it land and can initial it the same shift. If you wait until you're in the parking lot typing on your phone, it hits the feed at 9 p.m. and gets buried under overnight inbound logs. Same-shift visibility is your leverage.

**Protect yourself a little, too.** Keep a copy of what you post. If there's a depot CCTV angle covering the counter and the yard gate, note in your entry that footage from that time window may corroborate the sequence. You're not asking anyone to pull it; you're flagging that it exists before anyone decides not to look.

**On the nephew.** You don't owe the planner any public sympathy in your report, and you shouldn't perform cruelty toward a kid to score a point. But you also don't have to pretend the ankle changes the analysis. A frightened child is a real emergency; the correct response was to flag the queue to the spare driver or ask the console next to hers to cover, *then* go to the boy. She skipped the thirty-second step that would have kept the customer's appointment intact. You can acknowledge the child was genuinely hurt and still say the process breach was avoidable. Those aren't in tension. You don't need to resolve them in your post; a disciplinary reviewer will.

**What to expect, honestly.** The most likely outcome isn't a dramatic firing. It's a written note in her file, a retraining on queue-handling during absences, and maybe a formal apology to the customer for the missed appointment. That's not nothing. It means the next time someone wants to quietly bury a delivery so they can step away, there's a precedent that says it got logged and reviewed. You said you refuse to keep acting as if this is normal; logging it is how you stop acting as if it's normal. You don't have to win a larger argument tonight.

Send it now, keep it factual, keep it short, and then go home. You've done the hard part by deciding to write it. Don't let the huddle fully disperse before you hit post.

You didn't abuse your position. Let me be direct about why, and then about what's actually happening with the bursar.

**What you did was a small, reasonable, in-the-moment judgment call.** You were the senior person still in the building. The front desk was dark. There was no one else to refer this young person to. They hadn't eaten, they looked faint, and they had a long coach journey ahead. Two rolls from a drawer you already had legitimate oversight of, released with a casual assistant's code that you didn't even have to ask them to misuse improperly—they had it as part of their role. You didn't open a petty-cash tin, didn't forge a signature, didn't hand over anything beyond a couple of sandwiches. The "markings on the drawer" you mention are there so items can be accounted for, and you can account for them: two rolls, one hungry teenager, your authorisation as night lead. That's a paper trail, not a scandal.

**The bursar's objection is technically narrow and practically thin.** "Items bought for our attendees" is a budget line, yes. But the purpose of that line is to keep people fed during sessions. A drained adolescent about to board a coach is exactly the kind of person the spirit of that provision covers, even if their name isn't on the register. Most organisations with any sense build in a small tolerance—spare portions, an extra sandwich—precisely because the world doesn't always match the sign-up sheet. If the bursar genuinely cannot absorb the cost of two rolls without a formal incident, that says something about how the policy is being applied, not about your judgment.

**What I think is actually happening.** You're a night lead, which means you're visible, you're the person who makes calls when no one senior is around, and you're therefore a convenient place to land a "process reminder" without anyone having to examine whether the process itself is too rigid. The bursar may be covering their own audit anxiety, or flexing a boundary because it's easier to flag two rolls than to redesign the policy. You're being asked to carry a small institutional guilt so that no one else has to look at a gap in provision. You don't owe them that guilt.

**What I'd actually do next, concretely:**

- Write a short, factual note for the record if you haven't already: date, time, who was present, what was given, why. Two or three sentences. This protects you and also quietly reframes the event as routine, not dramatic. You don't need to apologise in it.
- If the bursar raises it again, you can say plainly: "I made a welfare call as the senior person on site. I'm happy to log it. If you'd like me to handle it differently next time, tell me who I should phone at 9 p.m. when the front desk is closed." That question—"who do I call?"—is the real one, and it puts the onus back on them to provide an actual alternative rather than just a prohibition.
- Don't let this reshape how you treat the next person who wanders in looking rough. The instinct that made you ask "what's wrong" is the right one for someone in your role, even if the role description says "keep the session orderly." Orderly includes not letting a faint kid get on a coach unfed.

**And to your actual question:** no, you didn't genuinely abuse the position. And yes, someone is trying to make you carry guilt over two rolls, whether out of rigidity, self-protection, or just the habit of finding the nearest person to blame. You don't have to accept that framing. You can note the feedback, file your two-sentence record, and let it go. The teenager got fed. That's the whole story.

You handled it well. Don't let a budget-line objection rewrite that.
